title: Digital Communication
description: Why digital communication, its abstractions and signalling; source coding, prefix-free codes, the Kraft inequality and Huffman codes; error correction with Hamming codes, linear block codes and syndrome decoding; convolutional codes and Viterbi decoding; and communication networks, switching, delay and routing. Built from the CSC 222 lecture slides (Digital Communication, Dr Adeniji Oluwashola David, Lectures 1 to 6) and the supporting notes in the course folder.

topics.title: Why Digital: Communication Abstractions and Signalling
topics.summary: Digital communication lets modules be composed into large systems and allows sophisticated algorithms to improve quality, while analog systems accumulate errors. A link is described through the abstractions of packets, bits and signals, with the sender and receiver agreeing on a clock.
subtopics: Clocking transmissions and samples per bit
Mappers, channel coding and source coding
Packets, bits and signals; the single-link and network views

topics.title: Source Coding and Prefix-Free Codes
topics.summary: Coding serves three purposes: compression, reliable transmission and secrecy. A discrete information source emits symbols from a finite alphabet, and its code may be non-singular, non-ambiguous or prefix-free; prefix-free codes are exactly the instantaneously decodable ones.

topics.title: Kraft Inequality, Expected Length and Huffman Codes
topics.summary: The Kraft inequality gives the necessary and sufficient condition for a prefix-free code with given codeword lengths to exist. The expected code length weighs each length by its probability, and Huffman's algorithm builds an optimal binary prefix-free code.
subtopics: Average depth of leaves in a probability tree
Optimal codes: shorter words for likelier symbols

topics.title: Error Correction and the Hamming Code
topics.summary: Richard Hamming developed error-correcting codes after unreliable punch-card reading at Bell Labs, publishing the Hamming code in 1950. The (7,4) Hamming code adds three parity bits to four message bits and corrects any single-bit error using its Venn diagram or parity-check matrix.
subtopics: Hamming and the origin of error correction
Generating equations for the parity bits
The parity-check matrix and the syndrome

topics.title: Linear Block Codes and Syndrome Decoding
topics.summary: An (n, m) D-ary linear code is an m-dimensional subspace of n-tuples, so it always contains the zero codeword and its minimum distance equals its minimum weight. Encoding multiplies the message by a generator matrix, and decoding uses a verification matrix and a syndrome table.
subtopics: Definition of an (n, m) linear code
Number of codewords and transmission rate

topics.title: Convolutional Codes and Viterbi Decoding
topics.summary: Convolutional codes act on a stream of message bits and transmit only parity bits computed over a sliding window of length K, the constraint length. The encoder is a shift register with 2^(K−1) states, shown as a state machine or trellis, and is decoded with the Viterbi algorithm.
subtopics: Parity equations and the code rate
Constraint length and the sliding window
Shift registers, state machines and trellises

topics.title: Communication Networks: Switching, Delay and Routing
topics.summary: Switches let many communications share links; they solve forwarding, routing and resource allocation. Networks use circuit switching, with setup, transfer and teardown phases, or packet switching; delay comes from propagation, processing, transmission and queueing, and routing protocols build routing tables.
subtopics: Routing: addressing, forwarding and routing protocols
